title: VC0-00646
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): They are appealing a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying their claim for refugee protection and are asking the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) to find them to be Convention refugees under s. 96 or persons in need of protection under s. 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (Act).
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (Principal Appellant) and XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX (Associate Appellants) are citizens of Colombia. They are appealing a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying their claim for refugee protection and are asking the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) to find them to be Convention refugees under s. 96 or persons in need of protection under s. 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (Act). The notice of decision was signed on January 15, 2020 and was received by the Appellants on January 21, 2020. a. According to their Basis of Claim (BOC), Appellant XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX) has been targeted by the "Aguilas Negras" (Black Eagles) because of his social activism with a XXXX XXXX organization as well as his political involvement in helping a candidate in an election. He also alleges that his father was threatened and assaulted because of his activities. The Appellants fear for their lives should they return to Colombia. b. The RPD rejected their claim of refugee protection for lack of credibility. It concluded that the Black Eagles did not have the means nor the motivation to target XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. c. In their Memorandum of Appeal, the Appellants submitted additional evidence about the Black Eagles. They argued that the RPD erred in its assessment of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX's credibility and omitted to conduct an analysis of under sections 96 and 97 of the Act. d. The determinative issue for the RAD is credibility.

Pursuant to Section 111(1)(a) of the Act, the RAD confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection. The appeals are dismissed. ADMISSIBILITY OF EVIDENCE SUBMITTED ON APPEAL

The Appellants submitted several newspaper articles with their Memorandum of Appeal. They argue that the evidence postdates the RPD's decision and as such, meets the requirements of subsection 110(4) of the Act. According to their submission, the evidence is material and relevant as it relates to the existence of the Black Eagles and their presence throughout Colombia.1

According to the law,2 I can only accept evidence that: i. arose after the RPD decision; or ii. was not reasonably available at the time of the decision; or iii. that you could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to bring to the RPD before the decision.
In the case of new evidence that post-dates the RPD's decision, I will assess the evidence based on the information it contains, and not only the date of the document.3
If the evidence meets one or more of the requirements set out in paragraph 4, I must decide if the evidence is new, credible and relevant before I can accept it.4

I find the news articles submitted by the Appellants are not admissible as new evidence. My reasons follow. Colombia: Paramilitary Black Eagles Threaten Social Activists, February 7, 2020: This article post-dates the RPD's decision. However, the article mentions threats against journalists and politicians in favor of national strikes. XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX is neither a journalist nor a politician and does not allege having any involvement with the organization or participation in national strikes. The article is therefore not relevant as it is incapable of proving any of the allegations made by the Appellants. It is not admissible on appeal because it does not meet the statutory requirements under ss. 110(4) of the Act and jurisprudence. End of Political Violence and Threats Advocated in Colombia, February 14; This article has no year of publication and it is not possible to determine if it post-dates the RPD's decision. While I note that it refers to an event taking place on October 11, 2019, the Appellants have not demonstrated that they were unable to obtain this article before the RPD's decision nor that they would not have reasonably been expected to provide the article before the RPD's decision. It is therefore not admissible on appeal in accordance with ss. 110(4) of the Act. Venezuelan Migrants Face Rising Xenophobia in Latin America, February 13, 2020; This article post-dates the RPD's decision. However, the information it contains did not arise after the RPD rejection and was reasonably available for the Appellants to present to the RPD. It is therefore not admissible in evidence as it does not meet the statutory requirements of ss. 110(4) of the Act. HRW: Armed Groups Move Freely on Colombia-Venezuela Border, January 22, 2020; This article about a Human Rights Watch Report post-dates the RPD's decision but it contains information about activities which took place before the decision. The evidence was reasonably available to present to the RPD. It is therefore not admissible as evidence because it does not meet the statutory requirements under ss. 110(4) of the Act. Everybody in Colombia Can Guess Who the Aguilas Negras Are, Except the Aguilas Negras, January 21, 2020; The article post-dates the RPD's decision. However, it does not meet the requirements of ss. 110(4) of the Act because the information it contains did not arise after the RPD rejection of the claim and was reasonably available for the Appellants to present to the RPD. It is therefore not admissible on appeal. Black Eagles, The Name with Which Criminals Are Camouflaged? February 6, 2020; This article post-dates the RPD's decision and contains information about threats made against the national leaders and militants of the FARC Party. However, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX is neither a national leader nor a militant of the FARC Party and therefore the article is not relevant to his claim. The evidence is not admissible on Appeal as it does not meet the requirements of ss. 110(4) of the Act nor the applicable jurisprudence. Teresita Gaviria, in the Sights of the Black Eagles, January 30, 2020; This article post-dates the RPD's decision but contains information about events which occurred before the RPD's decision. It does not meet the requirements of ss. 110(4) of the Act because the information it contains did not arise after the RPD rejection of the claim and was reasonably available for the Appellants to present to the RPD. It is therefore not admissible as evidence. Request for hearing

The Appellants submit that the RPD based its decision on negative credibility findings and that, based on the news articles about the existence of the Black Eagles included with their Memorandum, the RAD should hold a hearing under ss. 110(6) of the Act.

Ss. 110(3) of the Act requires that the RAD proceed without a hearing, on the basis of the RPD's record, while allowing the RAD to accept documentary evidence and submissions from the Minister and the Appellants. The person, who is the subject of the appeal may, pursuant to ss. 110(4) of the Act, present only evidence that arose after the rejection of their claim or that was not reasonably available, or that the person could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented, at the time of the rejection.

According to ss. 110(6) of the Act, upon which the Appellants rely, the RAD may hold a hearing if, in its opinion, there is documentary evidence referred to in ss. 110(3) of the Act of the that raises a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the Appellants, that is central to the RPD's decision, and that, if accepted, would justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim. In this appeal, the documentary evidence referred to in ss. 110(3) of the Act must be understood in relation to ss. 110(4) of the Act.

When read together, ss. 110(3), (4) and (6) of the Act establish that the RAD must not hold a hearing in an appeal such as this unless there is new evidence, in which case the RAD may hold a hearing if that new evidence raises a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the Appellants, is central to the RPD's decision, and that, if accepted, would justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim.
As no new evidence has been accepted as admissible by the RAD, I must proceed without a hearing. The Appellants' request for an oral hearing is denied.

The RAD reviews RPD decisions on a standard of correctness. In limited circumstances, the RPD may have a meaningful advantage over the RAD in assessing evidence that was before the RPD. In those cases, the RAD will show deference to the RPD. In this appeal, I have applied the correctness standard unless specifically stated otherwise.5

Based on my independent analysis of the evidence, including my reading of the transcript of the hearing before the RPD, I do not find that the RPD erred. What follows are my reasons. The Black Eagles as agents of persecution

In its decision, the RPD found that based on credible and undisputed documentary evidence, more particularly in the National Documentation Package (NDP), the Black Eagles do not have a central leadership, a central command nor a defined structure like other paramilitary organizations. They are unstable and there is little evidence to suggest that they operate like a systemic organization. In summary, the RPD concluded that the Black Eagles "is not nearly the force that you [XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX] claim it to be".6
In their Memorandum, the Appellants allege that their agent of harm is the Black Eagles and that risks need not emanate only from groups that have a "central leadership".

The courts have established that for there to be a serious possibility of persecution, the agent of harm must have the means and the motivation.7 While I understand the Appellants' argument, in the case at hand, I believe that the RPD is correct in its determination that the Black Eagles' lack of dominant presence, command and structure and territorial control make it unable to target and reach a particular individual.

Because of the credibility issues that I will deal with below, I find that there is insufficient evidence, on a balance of probabilities, to prove that the Black Eagles have the capacity or desire to target and harm the Appellants. In fact, the documentary evidence on file, including that provided by the Appellants before the RPD, indicates that the name "Black Eagles" can be used by anyone engaging in criminal activity, including street gangs. Threatening pamphlet

XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX alleged having received a threatening pamphlet in XXXX 2017. He testified that he did not bring it to the attention of the police because he did not consider it serious enough to report. He also did not mention it to XXXX nor his family because he did not want them to feel threatened by its contents. He then testified that he continued his activities despite the alleged threat. The RPD found these explanations to be unreasonable.

In their Memorandum, the Appellants submit that XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX felt compelled to continue his political and social activism because of the nature of that activism and how he felt it was important.8

With respect, at the hearing, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX testified that he continued the work because he enjoyed the work, not because he felt compelled to continue.9 The Appellants submit in their Memorandum that there is no obligation on a refugee claimant to cease political or social activism to demonstrate that his fears are legitimate. While I agree there is no obligation, I do find that continuing work for the sake of enjoyment, after having received threats to his and his family's lives for the sake of his personal enjoyment, undermines XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX's credibility about the seriousness of the threats he alleges having received.

Not reporting the threatening pamphlet because, according to XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, he did not take it seriously, contradicts his allegations in his BOC that he felt his life was threatened. Such conduct also undermines his allegation that he could not rely on police protection. It is also unreasonable for XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, who views the threat seriously to include it as part of the basis of his refugee claim, but does not share any of the information with his family so it may protect itself nor with XXXX so that it may take the appropriate measures to protect its member.

In their Memorandum, the Appellants argue that police protection against the Black Eagles is not available but have not provided any persuasive evidence to that effect. For instance, when XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX's father testified about the highway attack that he was a victim of, he added that his complaint to police was rejected for lack of evidence and that he was unable to provide details about the incident. In the case of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, he chose in one instance not to report the threatening pamphlet to police. In another instance, when he was attacked in his mother's car, he did not disclose all of the information to police, more particularly that he had received threats related to his social and political activities. In my view, the evidence, both testimonial and documentary, does not support the Appellants' argument that there is no police protection in Colombia against the Black Eagles.

The RPD's finding that the failure of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX to have revealed the contents of the threatening pamphlet to the police, XXXX and his family undermines his credibility as to the seriousness of the threat is correct. Omissions in a complaint to the police and the Appellant's BOC

XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX testified that he was stopped by the police who told him to stop his political activities and social activism. Asked by the RPD why this important information was not mentioned in his complaint to the police,10 XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX replied that was what the general prosecutor wrote down. Asked by the RPD as to why this information was not in his BOC,11 XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. replied that at the time of filling out his BOC, he "did not realize everything".12

These explanations are not satisfactory. To begin with, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX has a XXXX education. He was able to read and understand the contents of the complaint. His signature also appears on the document. It is unlikely that the general prosecutor would not write down such important information in the complaint. XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX did not demonstrate that he had taken the necessary steps to have all the information put down in writing in his complaint by the prosecutor general. These unreasonable explanations regarding the missing information in his complaint undermine his credibility.

As for his BOC, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX affirmed at the outset of his hearing that it was complete, true and correct.13 Where a refugee claimant fails to mention important facts in his or her BOC, this may legitimately be considered by the Board to be an omission that goes to lack of credibility.14 I find that the information omitted from XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX's BOC is central to his refugee claim, namely that he is at risk because of his political activities and social activism. This omission is important and undermines his credibility. Attacks against the Appellant's Father

XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX's father alleged that he was involved in two incidents involving the Black Eagles. The first one happened when he was being stopped on the highway eight hours away from home and threatened by the Black Eagles because of his son's political and social activities. XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX has not provided any persuasive evidence of how such an attack could take place eight hours away from his father's home by an organization without any command structure nor regional control.

The second incident occurred when his father was attacked on his motorcycle and threatened because of his son's activities. However, at the time of the alleged incident, his son, already left the country.

Given the lack of persuasive evidence about the ability of the Black Eagles to carry out the alleged attacks, the RPD's conclusion that XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX's father was in fact a victim of random criminal violence in both incidents is correct. XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX returned to Colombia after failing to seek asylum in USA

XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX travelled to the USA in XXXX 2018 and stayed there until XXXX 2018, when he decided to return to Colombia. Asked by the RPD why he returned to the country where his alleged agents of persecution operated, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX replied that he had hoped that things had settled down. The RPD found this explanation, in light of the death threats that he had allegedly received, unreasonable and that it undermined his credibility. I agree with the RPD. By returning to a country in which he received death threats, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX was in fact getting closer to his agents of persecution who threatened his life and that of his family. His actions and unsatisfactory explanations for returning to Colombia undermine his credibility.

XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX also testified not having claimed asylum in the USA while he was there for a period of 4 months because he did not think of it. While failure to claim refugee status may not be in itself decisive, it is a relevant element that the RPD can take into account when assessing the credibility of an applicant as it is reasonable to expect that an applicant would make a claim at the first possible opportunity.15 The failure to do so has consistently been held by the Courts to indicate a lack of subjective fear and thus undermine an applicant's credibility because it can be construed as inconsistent with the behaviours of someone who genuinely fears for his life.16 In the case at hand, given the lack of a satisfactory explanation for not claiming asylum, the RPD reasonably drew an adverse inference as to XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX's credibility.
Failure to provide documentation

The RPD asked XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX to see the original documents in support of his allegations. XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX replied that he had left them in Colombia because he did not want to travel with them. The RPD found this explanation unreasonable and decided that it undermined his credibility.17

Article 11 of the Refugee Protection Division Rules states that claimants must provide acceptable documents establishing the elements of their claim. In absence of the documents, the claimant must explain why he has not provided the documents and what steps were taken to obtain them. For instance, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX did not provide any documentary evidence of his membership in a political party or the work he was allegedly carrying out for the candidate, XXXX XXXX.

XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX arrived in Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2019 while the hearing took place on December 23, 2019. This XXXX XXXX XXXX period between his arrival and the hearing provided him ample time to have the documents sent to Canada. Absent any effort to retrieve the documents during this period or any explanation as to why no efforts were made, I find that the RPD's decision that this undermined his credibility to be correct.

On the basis of the findings noted above and after its own assessment of all the evidence in the record, including the transcript of the hearing, the RAD agrees with the RPD's finding that the Appellants have not established, on a balance of probabilities, that their agent of persecution, the Black Eagles, has the desire or the ability to put their lives or safety in peril should they return to Colombia. The RAD further finds that the Appellants have not established, on a balance of probabilities, that they were threatened with harm by individuals in Colombia because of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX's social activism and political activities.

Therefore, the RAD finds that there is not a serious possibility of persecution should the Appellants return to Colombia. The RAD therefore concludes that the Appellants have failed to establish a well-founded fear of persecution under section 96 of the Act, and, for the same reasons, the RAD finds that the Appellants are not persons in need of protection or at a risk to life, or at risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or in danger of torture as set out in section 97 of the Act.

Pursuant to Section 111(1)(a) of the Act, the RAD confirms the decision of the RPD that XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX are neither Convention refugees under section 96 nor persons in need of protection under section 97 of the Act.

The appeals are dismissed. (signed) Nicole Ladouceur Nicole Ladouceur February 1, 2021 Date 1 P-2, Appeal record, Memorandum of Appeal, at pages 30-31. 2 Subsection 110(4) of the Act. 3 Jadallah v.
